Diagnoses/summary: Combined generalised and focal epilepsy type – patient reports features of both generalised seizures (brief absences and occasional generalised tonic–clonic events) and focal aware/aware-impaired episodes with temporal features. Seizure frequency currently reported as ≤ 6 to 7 per year, typically clustering around periods of jet lag and sleep loss related to frequent business travel across time zones. He reports his seizure burden remains ≤ 6 to 7 per year, with a recognisable pattern: brief focal aware episodes with déjà vu and epigastric rising lasting under a minute, and rarer generalised tonic–clonic seizures typically following multiple long-haul flights. Current medicines:
- Lamotrigine 150 mg twice daily
- Brivaracetam 100 mg twice daily (initiated abroad three months ago; self-reported better tolerability than levetiracetam)
- Clobazam 10 mg at night PRN for travel weeks (1–3 nights around long-haul flights)
- Riboflavin 200 mg daily for migraine prophylaxis (self-initiated)

Travel and lifestyle context: Works across Europe, the US, and Asia with frequent time zone shifts. Uses airline pre-boarding to reduce stress, wears medical ID, and adheres to local driving restrictions when abroad. Plan:
- Continue lamotrigine and brivaracetam at current doses given tolerability and seizure frequency of ≤ 6 to 7 per year. Reinforced adherence strategies during flight disruptions (carry-on blister packs, duplicate alarm prompts, and setting local-time conversion reminders).
- Clobazam PRN limited to travel-associated high-risk periods; advised on sedation risk and avoidance of alcohol when used.
- Agreed to trial structured sleep hygiene across time zones (patient-led): maintaining dark/light cues, limiting late caffeine, and scheduling short naps on arrival days based on local time; patient prefers non-pharmacological measures.
- Safety: reiterated water precautions, working at height, and local regulations for driving post-seizure when abroad; patient confirms compliance.
- Investigations: No immediate further imaging required. If breakthrough frequency increases or semiology changes, consider prolonged ambulatory EEG to characterise both generalised and focal events during travel periods.
- Follow-up: Telephone review in 4 months or earlier if two or more events occur within a month. Patient will forward seizure diary screenshots monthly via secure portal.

- Agreed to continue clobazam PRN for short clusters only and to maintain a detailed seizure diary noting sleep, meals, and stressors.
- Provided information on local peer support groups; he will explore options that fit his routine to mitigate social isolation.

Follow-up:
- Telephone review by epilepsy nurse in 6–8 weeks to check diary, adherence, and side effects if any changes occur.
- Face-to-face clinic review in 3–4 months or sooner if events increase in intensity, duration, or lead to injury.
- Emergency plan discussed: seek urgent help if an event lasts longer than 5 minutes or if there are repeated events without full recovery.

No confirmed cardiac or metabolic precipitants identified to date.

- Given the predominantly nocturnal pattern and partner-reported events, I have requested a home video-EEG with overnight emphasis and ambulatory ECG patch monitoring to evaluate for ictal versus non-epileptic nocturnal events and to exclude significant arrhythmia.
- Sleep assessment: Referral to sleep clinic for possible obstructive sleep apnoea assessment given snoring and unrefreshing sleep, which may exacerbate events.
- Safety advice discussed: nocturnal supervision where possible, padded bed edges, avoid sleeping at height, and morning showering rather than bathing when alone.
- Seizure diary to continue, with specific note of timing relative to sleep, stress, illness, and missed doses. Patient encouraged to obtain smartphone audio/video if safe when events are suspected.
- Bloods to screen for contributory factors: morning prolactin within 30–60 minutes of an observed event if feasible; repeat U&E and LFT prior to any future medication changes.

- DVLA and safety reiterated; patient already not driving and will inform DVLA as appropriate depending on outcomes.
- Follow-up: nurse specialist call in 6–8 weeks to review frequency (aim remains to track seizures every other week pattern) and tolerability of current approach; clinic review in approximately 3 months, sooner if events escalate or daytime episodes occur.

Thank you for asking me to review your patient, whom I saw in clinic today, accompanied by her partner and an assistance dog in training provided through a charitable programme. She reports that her habitual events have persisted over the last year and she has begun logging them with a menstrual tracking app to better understand timing. She notes that the attacks cluster around her period, with the window of vulnerability beginning a few days prior to bleeding and extending into the early days thereafter. Outside that peri-period interval, she seldom experiences events. She describes this pattern as “most episodes falling from roughly three days before the period up to three days afterwards,” which her partner’s observations broadly corroborate.

The typical spell begins without warning, with a brief pause in activity and a blank facial expression. This is followed by loss of responsiveness and stiffening of both arms with a low vocal sound; on some occasions there is bilateral shaking lasting under two minutes. She is usually tired and mildly confused for 30–60 minutes afterwards, sometimes with headache. She denies clear nocturnal events, tongue biting or urinary incontinence, and has no consistent focal neurological symptoms pre- or post-event. She reports no recent head injury, febrile seizures in childhood, or family history of similar episodes. Sleep deprivation and marked stress may lower her threshold, but alcohol does not appear to be a trigger. She is not currently driving.

Medication history: she is taking lamotrigine 150 mg twice daily without reported rash, and folic acid 5 mg daily. She has previously tried levetiracetam for six months but discontinued due to irritability. No known drug allergies. She uses a period-tracking diary and has begun aligning her logs with her partner’s notes and smartwatch detections of elevated heart rate during events; these data suggest the cyclical clustering described above.

Examination in clinic today was unremarkable with normal cranial nerves, tone, power, coordination and gait. Cardiovascular and respiratory examinations were normal. There were no signs of depression on brief screen, though she describes intermittent anxiety around the time of anticipated episodes. The assistance dog in training remained calm and did not interfere with the assessment; she reports the dog has been conditioned to alert her partner when she becomes unresponsive, which has improved safety at home.

Prior investigations: routine EEG six months ago was within normal limits. MRI brain (1.5T) last year was reported as structurally normal. Bloods including U&E, LFT, glucose, thyroid function and prolactin (post-event sampling not obtained) have been unremarkable. Cycle tracking notes were shown on her phone and suggest the temporal clustering stated above.

Impression: ongoing recurrent events with a clear temporal association to the menstrual cycle as described. At present I cannot provide a single unifying classification of the events from the information available. The pattern and witness accounts warrant further characterisation.

Plan:
- I have requested ambulatory EEG with event button capture timed across the late luteal to early follicular phase next cycle, as she reliably experiences events within that interval. 
- Repeat high-resolution MRI brain (3T) with epilepsy protocol to be arranged.
- Continue lamotrigine 150 mg twice daily for now; she prefers to avoid changes until after the monitoring period. She understands the importance of strict adherence and will continue to log events.
- Safety advice reinforced: avoid baths unsupervised, consider showering with door unlocked, caution with heights and open water, and continue partner supervision during higher-risk days as per her log. The assistance dog training team will be informed (with her consent) of monitoring dates so they can support exposure in a controlled manner.
- I have provided a seizure first aid leaflet and discussed SUDEP risk in simple terms; she is aware of the benefit of regular sleep and stress management.
- We discussed that if the cyclical pattern is consistently demonstrated on monitoring, we could explore time-targeted strategies in liaison with her GP and gynaecology colleagues.

I will review her in clinic after the ambulatory EEG and MRI are completed. Please let me know if I can provide any further information. Thank you again for involving me in her care.

Thank you for referring this patient for neurological review. I met him today in clinic accompanied by his partner. He described longstanding episodes that he and his family have termed “spells,” beginning in his late teens. The events are stereotyped: he experiences a brief warning of a rising internal tension and a sense of detachment, followed by behavioural arrest with fixed gaze and lip chewing reported by witnesses. On some occasions there is right arm stiffening and a brief cry. He is typically confused for 15–30 minutes afterwards and complains of a throbbing headache with pronounced fatigue.

Regarding periodicity, he and his partner report that the events tend to group together over several days in a repeating pattern roughly every four to five weeks. Within these burst periods the number of episodes varies and has not been reliably logged; outside these periods he may go a week or two without events. This “regular bursts every few weeks; number during bursts not well documented” pattern has been their usual experience for years. He started levetiracetam six months ago after trials of lamotrigine and carbamazepine were discontinued for rash and dizziness respectively. Notably, since commencing current therapy the overall pattern has persisted without clear change in frequency or recovery time.

There is no consistent relationship with sleep deprivation or alcohol, though he suspects that high work stress and missed meals may act as triggers. No tongue laceration or incontinence has been witnessed. He has had two emergency attendances in the last year for cluster days with prolonged confusion; bloods at those times were unremarkable and a CT head performed three years ago was reported normal. He has never had status epilepticus or significant injury from these events. Family history is non-contributory. He does not drive and is aware of DVLA guidance as previously discussed with his GP.

On examination today he was alert and oriented with normal speech, cranial nerves intact, no focal motor deficit, and normal coordination and gait. Cardiovascular and general examination were unremarkable. There were no features of ongoing post-event confusion at the time of review. Blood pressure 126/78 mmHg, pulse 72 bpm regular.

We discussed next steps. The main issue at present is to clarify the nature of the events and obtain objective correlation. He is agreeable to an ambulatory EEG with event diary, followed by consideration of inpatient video-EEG if the ambulatory study does not capture typical episodes. I have also recommended structured documentation using a calendar or smartphone app to record the timing of warning symptoms, event duration, and recovery features, so that we can quantify numbers during the clustered periods. He will continue levetiracetam at his current dose as he reports tolerability but no perceived benefit so far; we will not change treatment until we have more diagnostic information. I have requested routine bloods (FBC, U&E, LFT, vitamin D) to be done at his GP surgery for baseline monitoring.

For safety, we reinforced standard advice around adequate sleep, regular meals, moderated alcohol intake, and seeking urgent help if any event lasts more than five minutes, occurs back-to-back without recovery, or if he sustains significant injury. He understands not to swim unsupervised, to avoid heights, and to take showers instead of baths.

I will review him in clinic after the ambulatory EEG. Thank you again for the referral and for your ongoing care. Please let me know if there is any additional history or prior imaging that would be helpful to obtain before telemetry.

Thank you for asking me to review this patient. He attended with his paper seizure calendar, which he updates daily and brings reliably to each visit. - Patient to maintain his paper seizure calendar, with particular attention to sleep duration and timing before and after travel.
- Follow-up in clinic after telemetry or sooner if there is any escalation in frequency or severity.

Recurrent unprovoked seizures; phenotype under ongoing evaluation

- Proceed with ambulatory EEG to characterise nocturnal clusters.  
- Maintain detailed seizure and mood/sleep diary; bring to next review.

Dear Dr Patel,

Epilepsy Diagnosis:

Combined generalised and focal epilepsy (patient reports both generalised and focal epilepsy).

Background and context:

He cycles to work most days and reports that his routine is relatively consistent; this has been recorded for context. No recent intercurrent illness or sleep deprivation was volunteered.

Current Medication:

1. Lamotrigine 150 mg twice daily
2. Brivaracetam 50 mg twice daily

- Topiramate (stopped due to cognitive slowing)
- Sodium valproate (stopped when planning family; weight gain reported)

Morning clusters one - two×/month; ~four events over 90 min. There have been no injuries reported during recent events.

Assessment and Plan of Action:

The pattern suggests persistent focal onset seizures with secondary generalisation within the context of combined generalised and focal epilepsy. Given partial response to lamotrigine and brivaracetam, I propose introducing lacosamide as adjunctive therapy and then reassessing. If tolerated, we will consider rationalising the regimen at follow-up.

Lacosamide titration schedule:
- Week 1: 50 mg at night
- Week 2: 50 mg twice daily
- Week 3: 50 mg in the morning and 100 mg at night
- Week 4: 100 mg twice daily (continue at this dose thereafter pending review)

Primary generalised epilepsy

7. Leave and appointments: Permit short-notice compassionate or carer’s leave when childcare issues arise. Support time off for medical appointments without penalising attendance records.
8. Training and awareness: Provide basic staff guidance on supporting employees with long-term neurological conditions, focusing on respectful communication and privacy.

He denies tongue-biting outside of the generalised events and has had two minor falls this year without injury. There is no current use of alcohol or recreational drugs, and he remains independent with activities of daily living. He has limited social contact but is open to community support should it be available.

Current anti-seizure medication is lamotrigine 150 mg twice daily, well tolerated without rash, dizziness, or diplopia. - Reinforce seizure diary and safety advice at home; provide written advice on when to seek urgent care.

Recurrent seizures of uncertain classification with variable frequency and severity

Remote history of mild traumatic brain injury noted; no definitive structural correlate identified to date

Seasonal allergic rhinitis managed with as-required non-sedating antihistamines; otherwise well

Combined generalised and focal epilepsy (patient has both generalised and focal epilepsy). 

Thank you for referring Michael O’Connor for pre-conception counselling. He attended clinic today with his partner. We reviewed his seizure history, current management, and considerations for pregnancy planning from a paternal perspective, including medication safety, driving, safety planning, and genetic counselling information.

- His first seizure occurred in January 2024 in Ireland, at night while asleep. He woke with rhythmic twitching of the right arm and a sense of déjà vu. The second and third event was in June 2024 in Scotland, also during sleep, lasting five minutes with a similar pattern of symptoms. 
- He also reports two lifetime episodes (both in 2023) of brief generalised myoclonic jerks on awakening after sleep deprivation, without loss of awareness, and one episode of probable generalised tonic–clonic seizure in adolescence after heavy alcohol intake (no medical review at the time). 
- Triggers identified: sleep deprivation and excess alcohol. No history of status epilepticus.

- MRI brain (epilepsy protocol) May 2024: no focal cortical dysplasia or hippocampal sclerosis identified; structurally normal study. 
- EEG April 2024: intermittent left temporal sharp waves during drowsiness; generalised 3–4 Hz spike–wave bursts provoked by hyperventilation, consistent with combined generalised and focal epilepsy. 
- Routine bloods (U&E, LFT, FBC, B12/folate, glucose) April 2024: within reference range.

- He is not yet on anti-seizure medication (ASM). We discussed first-line options suitable for combined generalised and focal epilepsy. Pre-conception counselling (paternal): 
- We discussed heritable risk: for idiopathic epilepsies the absolute risk to offspring is modestly increased compared to background but remains low overall; precise risk depends on the final syndromic classification. - ASM considerations: if medication is initiated, a broad-spectrum agent with favourable teratogenic profile for partners planning pregnancy was discussed. We outlined the need to avoid sodium valproate. He was advised on adherence, sleep optimisation, and minimising alcohol. 
- Safety: night-time supervision strategies, seizure first aid for partner, and avoidance of high-risk activities (heights, open water, operating heavy machinery) until seizure control is established. DVLA guidance was explained: following nocturnal seizures he must meet regulations for driving; he has currently stopped driving and will follow medical advice and statutory periods. 

Plan: 
1) Provide written information on paternal pre-conception counselling, SUDEP, and seizure first aid. 
2) Sleep hygiene and alcohol reduction measures. 
3) Arrange sleep-deprived EEG in 6–8 weeks to characterise interictal abnormalities during drowsiness and sleep. 
4) If further seizures occur or if he and his partner proceed with pregnancy plans sooner, we will commence a broad-spectrum ASM after shared decision-making; emergency access advice provided. 
5) Liaise with primary care for workplace risk assessment support and DVLA notification guidance. 
6) Follow-up in 3 months, sooner if breakthrough events occur. He and his partner have contact details for our epilepsy nurse specialist.

Subject: Review and medication adjustment

Hi Thomas

Epilepsy Diagnosis:

Focal epilepsy (patient has focal epilepsy with probable temporal lobe onset, with occasional secondary generalisation reported by partner)

Present Medication:

1. Lamotrigine 150 mg twice daily
2. Brivaracetam 50 mg twice daily

Present Seizure Frequency:

He can sometimes go nearly two week without seizures, but when they recur he tends to have several in one day, often between 4 and 6. His partner notes brief focal aware auras (epigastric rising sensation and déjà vu) preceding most events, followed by impaired awareness episodes lasting 60–90 seconds. No clear triggers identified aside from poor sleep and missed evening doses on two occasions.

Plan of Action:

The history and witness accounts are in keeping with focal epilepsy, likely temporal lobe. Adverse mood effects have been mild on brivaracetam, and lamotrigine has been well tolerated. Given the clustering pattern and breakthrough events, I recommend a cautious titration of brivaracetam while maintaining lamotrigine, alongside rescue planning for clusters.

Please adjust brivaracetam as follows: increase to 75 mg twice daily for two weeks, then to 100 mg twice daily ongoing if tolerated. Continue lamotrigine 150 mg twice daily unchanged. We discussed adherence, sleep hygiene, and safety. I have provided a seizure diary template and advised the patient to record auras and any potential precipitating factors. I have also issued a buccal midazolam 10 mg rescue plan for clusters exceeding three focal impaired-awareness seizures within two hours, as per local protocol.

I will review him in clinic in three months. If seizure control improves without adverse effects, we will consider a slow lamotrigine up-titration or EEG/MRI review if clusters persist. The patient understands DVLA guidance and is currently not driving.

Seizure disorder under ongoing evaluation; pattern and semiology remain under investigation

Generalised anxiety symptoms related to travel; seasonal allergic rhinitis managed with over‑the‑counter antihistamines

He works in a manual, safety‑sensitive environment involving heights and machinery, and both he and his employer have noticed episodes at or around workdays that are impacting his attendance and confidence.

We also discussed sleep hygiene, regular medication timing for any future treatments, and keeping a seizure diary to document clusters and potential triggers.

I will update you following telemetry and imaging, and we can then consider appropriate therapy and rescue strategies for clusters if indicated. Please let me know if there are additional details from the workplace observations that would help inform the diagnostic work‑up.

Thank you for asking me to review this gentleman. We conducted a planned telephone consultation while he was onshore between offshore rotations. He reports a longstanding history of generalised epilepsy. He may go four to five days without seizures, but when they happen he often has them in batches, with two - three occurring within 24 hours. He and his partner describe typical events as abrupt loss of awareness with generalised stiffening and rhythmic jerking lasting around 60–90 seconds, followed by post-ictal confusion for up to 30 minutes. He occasionally bites his tongue and has had one shoulder strain in the past but no recent injuries. There is no consistent focal onset aura reported.

He works offshore on a two-weeks-on, two-weeks-off rotation. Seizures tend to cluster either at the end of a run of night shifts or within the first 48 hours after returning onshore, which he attributes to sleep disruption and variable meal times. He denies alcohol excess and states he avoids caffeine late in the day. He uses a medication alarm and a written seizure log while offshore. Occupational Health have placed him on restricted duties when offshore; he confirms he does not undertake safety-critical tasks on days following a seizure.

He is currently taking valproate 1,000 mg twice daily and levetiracetam 1,500 mg twice daily with good adherence. No clear adverse effects are reported beyond mild irritability during periods of poor sleep. He has rescue buccal midazolam available but has not needed to use it in the last three months. He has not driven and understands DVLA regulations. He last had a generalised tonic–clonic seizure 10 days ago, with two events occurring the same day, and none since.

Impression: Generalised epilepsy with clustering related to sleep disruption and rota transitions. Current regimen is broadly effective with intermittent breakthrough clusters as described above. We discussed optimising sleep hygiene during shift transitions and maintaining strict regularity of doses while offshore. He prefers to continue the present regimen for now. We agreed to continue telephone reviews when he is onshore, with the option of bringing him for a routine EEG update in the next 6–9 months if breakthrough clusters increase. He will contact the clinic sooner if he experiences prolonged seizures, increased frequency, or any injuries.

- Continue valproate 1,000 mg twice daily and levetiracetam 1,500 mg twice daily.
- Maintain rescue midazolam for prolonged seizures (>5 minutes) and cluster management per prior plan.
- Reinforce sleep and shift-transition strategies; continue seizure diary.
- Occupational Health restrictions to remain unchanged offshore.
- Telephone review during his next onshore period in approximately 8–10 weeks, or earlier if seizures escalate.

- Levetiracetam 1 g twice daily
- Clobazam 10 mg at night PRN for clusters (used approximately twice monthly)

Adverse effects: reports irritability on levetiracetam mitigated somewhat with dose timing and exercise; otherwise tolerating regimen. No recent injuries. He remains abstinent from alcohol on working weeks and drinks minimal caffeine.

Examination today: Neurological examination normal. Weight stable, BMI 24. No focal deficits. Blood pressure 122/76.

Investigations: U&Es, LFTs, FBC from August 2025 normal; Vitamin D borderline low (51 nmol/L). No evidence of hyponatraemia. ECG last year normal sinus rhythm.

Discussion/Plan:
- We discussed that his pattern and investigations support a diagnosis of combined generalised and focal epilepsy. We reviewed the role of sleep and circadian stability; he is a rotating shift worker including nights and feels the night-to-day swing is the principal precipitant of clusters.
- Medication: continue Lamotrigine 150 mg BD. Reduce Levetiracetam to 750 mg BD trial if mood symptoms persist after we implement sleep measures; if seizures worsen, revert to 1 g BD. Follow-up: Epilepsy nurse telephone follow-up in 6 weeks to review shift adjustments, mood, and cluster frequency; clinic review in 4 months or earlier if clusters increase in frequency or if he has any generalised seizures despite improved sleep strategy.
